Last week, CRWV announced two new deals, one with Meta for an incremental \$21B , and another with Anthropic for an undisclosed amount (we presume it is not large, but still a meaningful new logo). Our thesis was always that CRWV and other neoclouds would do fine in the near term, with longer-term issues to come, but we will concede that the company has exceeded our early 2026 expectations. We maintain our Under-Perform, but raise our target price to \$67 on the new signings.
These deals don’t come in a vacuum - almost daily, we are catching headlines of someone signing or building or funding new data center capacity to meet demand. Our perspective continues to be that we are in a capacity land grab, and that that isn’t going to last forever. We are forecasting an easing of data center capacity in 2028 - maybe 2029 if you’re extremely bullish on AI demand.
Over the long-term, all hyperscalers will have hybrid approaches to capacity needs. But GWs aren’t all equal - we believe the prioritization will be:
1. Own as much real estate as you can where it makes sense - long-term workloads, inference use cases, markets where there is enough demand to justify owning your own building
2. Lease full buildings (powered shell) where you need to trade off capex for opex, need faster capacity than you can build, and/or have attractive economics or strong development partners
3. Fill in with smaller real estate leases (wholesale colo) where you have specific market needs but long-term visibility into requirements and can’t justify a full building
4. Use traditional cloud (if appropriate) or neocloud as a band-aid when you can’t get capacity fast enough, need it in a specific location that they happen to have, are not sure you will need a long-term workload in that location, and/or want to trial deployments in a sandbox before committing to your own build
In our current land grab state, options 1-4 are happening, but as things start to ease (not yet), we maintain our conviction that the fourth category (neocloud) is the fastest and worst hit. It’s far easier to churn out of a neocloud relationship than a data center - the contracts are shorter and you don’t have to move any hardware.
Eventually the LLM strategy should be similar to hyperscale, but today, these megaliths are bypassing Option #1 (and often Option #2) as they can’t yet support large-scale facility ownership or builds. They also are consuming significant capacity from traditional clouds - both GPUs and CPUs.
All of this underpins our call on CRWV (UP, \$67), and our long-term bearishness on the neocloud sector, though we anticipate continuing to see stock pops on news updates for many months to come.

INVESTMENT IMPLICATIONS CoreWeave (UP, \$67): We are Underperform on CRWV with a revised price target of \$67. We value the company using an EV/Adj. EBIT multiple (28.4x) on 2027 E Adj. EBIT per share of \$5.81. Our case hinges on our longer-term revenue expectations for CRWV, which are significantly lower than street expectations. In general, we question CRWV’s ability to continue to sign large-scale hyperscale deals as data center supply becomes more readily available (2028+) and are concerned that hyperscalers are likely to attempt head-on competition with neoclouds for enterprise business. We disagree with CRWV’s premise that its existing software moat will hold up to hyperscaler attacks, especially given hyperscalers’ scale and ability to spend. We do not believe the structural concerns abate with increased AI demand, though the timing for our call may be pushed further out. Importantly, we do not believe the tide will shift for CRWV in the very near term and anticipate them signing an incremental \$45B of deals between now and the end of 2027. We are roughly in line with consensus for 2026 expectations. By 2027, we begin to diverge, and by 2028, we are \~15% below consensus revenue estimates, accelerating through the forecast window. Since our last model refresh, we have increased our Price Target by \$11, reflecting a Meta deal that exceeded expectations and the promise of Anthropic revenue (numbers not disclosed). We have accordingly slowed margin improvement and increased capex. Finally, we have taken CRWV’s recent senior notes offering into account. DLR (OP, \$218): Outperform on a differentiated growth and de-risked development story, underpinned by a stable hyperscaler revenue floor, underappreciated enterprise upside driven by global interconnection density (with strong growth in the <1MW segment), and a capital-light development strategy that supports a durable valuation. Our \$218 price target is based on 26x our 2027E AFFO per share of \$8.31. EQIX (OP, \$1,128): Outperform on a long-term enterprise capacity reset, supported by its best-in-class interconnection ecosystem and metro footprint, with upside driven by a renewed build cadence and improving visibility into future capacity growth—albeit partially offset by near-term capex intensity and a measured contribution from xScale. Our \$1,128 price target is based on 25x our 2027E AFFO per share of \$44.92. MSFT (OP, \$641): Microsoft made a ‘big bet’ on Azure, investing aggressively in a global footprint and technology innovation. Starting in \~CY2019 they doubled down on their existing AI investment as they prepared for and added Gen AI capabilities, built AI datacenters and invested in their own chips. Despite a slight miss to buy side whisper number last quarter, Microsoft’s growth engine is in fact getting stronger given solid Azure growth and impressive RPO growth, and we expect Azure growth to accelerate near term (Microsoft: Could the bear case in fact be the bull case?). We also believe Microsoft is strongly positioned in the case of an AI bubble because their first-party usage of capacity is ramping thanks to their diversified app base, along with third-party contracts which comes from not only OpenAI but a diversified large enterprise customer base, and contract duration is well aligned with useful life of the equipment. While most of software is slowing, Azure is stable and will, we believe, accelerate supporting Microsoft’s strong double-digit revenue growth and GAAP margins in the mid 40s. We like the setup and see the current valuation as an attractive entry point. 2 on 14-Apr-2026 Madison Rezaei    +1 917 344 8622  madison.rezaei@bernsteinsg.com 14 April 2026 US COMMUNICATIONS INFRASTRUCTURE BERNSTEIN|SOCIETE CENERALECROUP

ORCL (OP, \$319): The Oracle story has shifted quickly from a potential Cloud and hyperscaler story to a major hyperscaler and AI training / inferencing provider. Oracle has \$553B in Remaining Performance Obligations (RPO) and exceptional OCI growth (\$166B in OCI revenue guidance for FY30), driven by multiple multi-billion dollar deals led by \~\$300B in RPO from OpenAI. This level of growth can potentially make OCI exceed GCP by CY29-30. Based on the work we have done on understanding the value of this transition (Oracle: The story is better than we thought, with better upside potential), we believe it would be highly value accretive. While near term this might impact margins and cash, it will likely drive very substantial earnings and FCF growth over the next 5–10 years. The stock has taken a beating over the last 6+ months due to various concerns, but we see the overhangs getting gradually clearer as Oracle has secured its financing though FY28/29, OpenAI raised another round funding, and OCI growth demonstrates strong execution.
We rate AMZN and META outperform. We rate GOOGL market-perform.

DETAILS
We have \~100GW of global data center supply today, and over the next 5 years, we expect the market size to reach \~190GW. For the AI bulls among us, we also model an upside case: \~220 GW by 2030. Regardless of where you ultimately fall out on AI and data center demand, nobody disagrees that the boom is currently full swing. Everyone wants GWs, as fast as they can possibly be built.
But it’s important to remember that all GWs are not the same. The capacity comes in different flavors, with different shelf-lives and levels of confidence - we think it’s important to pay attention to those differences as megadeals continue to be announced. If you are an AMZN, MSFT, or GOOG, you generally prefer to start at the left of this table and work right, solving for financial pressures and strategy.

HYPERSCALER-OWNED REAL ESTATE
Over the last 5 years, hyperscalers (AMZN, GOOG, META, MSFT, ORCL) have prolifically built data center capacity. Today, we estimate that they own \~40 GW globally, with an announced \~30 GW of incremental self-owned capacity to come online through 2030. This could easily accelerate through the forecast period as land banks expand and capex levels continue to rise.
For hyperscalers such as Google, Microsoft, Meta, and AWS, capital expenditures (CapEx) and property, plant, and equipment (PP&E) reflect the core mechanism through which cloud capacity, AI compute, and digital services are scaled. Hyperscale data centers are among the most capital-intensive assets in the global economy, requiring continuous, large-scale investment in land, purpose-built facilities, electrical and cooling infrastructure, networking equipment, and compute hardware. CapEx represents the primary vehicle by which hyperscalers convert operating cash flow into long-lived productive assets. These expenditures are capitalized onto the balance sheet as PP&E and include both infrastructure CapEx (e.g., buildings, power systems, shells) and technology CapEx (e.g., servers, storage, and networking gear). As a result, sustained increases in CapEx directly translate into PP&E growth, particularly during periods of accelerated cloud demand, AI model training cycles, or geographic expansion.
Given the heavy weighting of PP&E toward servers and networking hardware with 3- to $6 ^ { 1 }$ -year depreciation lives, depreciation expense is elevated and a material portion of CapEx is required just to refresh existing capacity. Accordingly, periods when CapEx meaningfully exceeds depreciation signal net increases in installed compute and future growth potential, while convergence toward depreciation implies a shift toward maintenance, efficiency, and utilization rather than incremental capacity build-out.

HYPERSCALER-LEASED REAL ESTATE
Augmenting the self-builds, hyperscalers have continued to sign huge leases with other data center providers. Though many have flipped private, we have seen major growth in CyrusOne, Switch, QTS, Vantage, Aligned, and other data centers focused specifically on hyperscale build-out.
Calculating forward-looking leased capacity on a per-hyperscaler basis is tricky - none of the leases are disclosed, there is wide variance in when things come online, and while you can attempt to back in looking at ESG numbers or via heroic assumptions on PP&E, we don’t have high confidence in either of those approaches. So for today, we will not attempt to differentiate who is leasing what over the long-term. Instead, we are looking at total builds targeted towards hyperscalers (overwhelmingly represented by the names on our list), and the 2025 estimates of owned v. leased capacity. Even looking in aggregate, it is clear there are big GW numbers allocated for each of these players.

HYPERSCALER CLOUD + NEOCLOUD LEASES
We’ve written at length about why we think hyperscalers do not continue to purchase capacity from neoclouds over the long term, but here is why we think we’re seeing leases like the large Meta deal:
1. Existing power capacity and speed to market: CRWV has legacy power from its mining days and has been aggressive about gobbling up incremental capacity via very long-term data center leases. We would argue that those leases were already passed up by hyperscalers themselves (generally a data center operator would prefer to have a hyperscale tenant), but regardless, CRWV has secured the capacity and can scale faster than a new building can be built.
2. Short-term commitments where visibility is cloudy: relative to building a data center or signing a 15-year lease, a 5- year deal with CRWV is a lot lower commitment (see our Situationship parallel). No one has perfect visibility into how AI requirements will evolve, so while hyperscalers are formulating their long-term plans, neoclouds represent a nice viable (if marginally more expensive) band-aid.
3. Sandbox and learning opportunities: CoreWeave is well-positioned as the largest AI focused pure-play and legitimately is the most sophisticated operator of a GPU cloud today - the hyperscalers want to use these clusters for trials and their own learnings before they deploy at scale.
Many investors have asked us about the strength of these contracts - can Meta default or cancel the \$21B if they ultimately don’t need the capacity? We have seen hyperscalers revise data center plans, manage for optionality, and temper formerly issued “bragawatt” statements. Meta has provisions in their Blue Owl Hyperion deal allowing for potential exit, Stargate thus far hasn’t lived up to (extremely high) expectations, and we all remember MSFT’s reshuffling in early 2025 that shook the whole industry. But at this time, we do not have reason to believe the CRWV-META contract is at risk.
Of course, we haven’t seen the lease, but are under the impression that the contracts are tight and “take or pay” committed GPU capacity, in line with CRWV’s prior contracts and statements. Since the company is leveraging these contracts for their DDTLs, we assume they are being carefully reviewed for outs. In this particular deal, Meta pays for guaranteed compute access regardless of usage levels, even if their internal data centers come online early, and CRWV cannot delay delivery without penalties. That doesn’t mean we have faith in a 2032 renewal.
